1	// PACKS THAT HAVE BEEN RENAMED — every legacy spelling, mapped straight to today's.
2	//
3	// A pack is activated by matching the id a member DECLARED against the id a pack
4	// module carries, literally. So the moment a canon pack's directory is renamed, every
5	// member's declaration is one cycle stale by construction, and a member holding the
6	// old spelling beside the new mount does not get a degraded pack — it gets NO pack,
7	// because nothing matches. For a pack carrying the `update` task that is terminal:
8	// the member loses the machinery that would have delivered its own repair, and the
9	// only route back in is a hand-run against each repo (#1004 is this failure with a
10	// smaller blast radius).
11	//
12	// The declaration rewrite still happens — the migration record converges every
13	// member onto today's spelling, so this map is a tolerance and not the mechanism.
14	// What the map buys is that no ORDERING of the two halves can strand anyone: a
15	// member reads correctly whether its declaration has been rewritten yet or not, and
16	// whether its mount is ahead of its declaration or behind it.
17	//
18	// STRAIGHT TO TODAY'S, never chained. A second rename of an already-renamed pack
19	// adds its oldest spelling here pointing at the newest name, so a declaration
20	// written for the very first vocabulary still normalizes in ONE pass — a chain of
21	// one-step hops would need as many passes as there have been renames, and every
22	// caller would have to know to loop.
23	//
24	// RETIREMENT is a convergence window, not a census, and the window is PER ENTRY: an
25	// entry comes out a week after `legacy-shape-in-use` starts reporting that spelling,
26	// which is the time a repo that converges nightly needs to read its own finding and
27	// rename its declaration. The canon cannot enumerate the repos that use it, so "when
28	// no member still declares it" is a condition nothing can ever answer — and until it
29	// is answered the map is load-bearing for exactly the repos that stopped converging.
30	// The seven spellings the 2026-08-19 renames and collapses left shared one window and
31	// came out together (#1641); what is here now landed after that advisory shipped, so
32	// each waits out its own week (#1909).
33	//
34	// A pack ABSORBED into another is the same map entry: its id resolves to the pack
35	// that now carries its rules, so a member declaring the absorbed one activates the
36	// survivor instead of activating nothing. The declaration then holds two ids that
37	// resolve to one, which is what `applyPackRenames` merges (registry.mjs).
38	// @legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-shape-in-use retire:#1909
39	export const RENAMED_PACKS = Object.freeze({
40	  // Absorbed, not renamed (#1681): the folder-access graph was never a pack anyone chose —
41	  // it carried no fingerprint and arrived through `requires` in every member that
42	  // declares the baseline — so its check, its contribution seam and its guide moved
43	  // into the pack that was already carrying it in.
44	  barriers: 'basics',
45	  // Absorbed too (#1839): the issue and PR sweeps were retired and the one tidy
46	  // dimension left — the weekly comment pass and the gate that bounds it — moved
47	  // into the baseline, so a member declaring the retired pack activates the pack
48	  // that now carries the pass rather than activating nothing.
49	  'tidy-repo': 'basics',
50	  // Renamed (#2101): the pack stopped carrying anything about how a site is built,
51	  // served or released and took the name of what it is about.
52	  'static-website': 'public-website',
53	});
54	
55	// The canon id a spelling resolves to. Canon packs only — a LOCAL pack lives in the
56	// member's own tree and its id is that repo's to choose, so a local pack that happens
57	// to be called `barriers` is a different pack than the canon one and must not be
58	// renamed out from under its owner.
59	export const canonicalPackId = (id) => RENAMED_PACKS[id] ?? id;
60	
61	// The id a CANON pack DIRECTORY contributes, given every raw id the same tree
62	// carries. The map cannot tell its two shapes apart, but the tree can:
63	//
64	//   RENAME    — one directory, whose `pack.mjs` may still carry the old id until
65	//               the mount is rewritten. Nothing else claims the new id, so the id
66	//               maps forward and the pack stays live.
67	//   ABSORPTION — the absorbed directory sits BESIDE its survivor's until a
68	//               converge lands. Mapping it forward would put two live
69	//               directories on one id, and the collision guard drops BOTH —
70	//               failing the converged tree's self-test, which parks the very
71	//               converge that would have removed the leftover (#1186).
72	//
73	// So an absorbed leftover keeps its own id and goes inert, which is what an id
74	// nothing declares is supposed to do. A member still declaring the absorbed
75	// spelling is unaffected: `canonicalPackId` resolves the DECLARATION onto the
76	// survivor, which is present and live.
77	export const canonicalPackIdAmong = (id, idsPresent) => {
78	  const to = canonicalPackId(id);
79	  return to !== id && idsPresent.has(to) ? id : to;
80	};
81	
82	// The same map over the keys of a stamp's `packVersions`. A renamed pack whose
83	// stamped version still sits under the old key reads as version-ABSENT, which is not
84	// a harmless miss: absent means "never installed", so the install flow claims it,
85	// stamps it at latest, and runs NO migration records — silently skipping every record
86	// in the gap the update flow would have applied.
87	export function canonicalPackVersions(packVersions) {
88	  if (!packVersions || typeof packVersions !== 'object') return packVersions;
89	  const out = {};
90	  for (const [id, version] of Object.entries(packVersions)) {
91	    const to = canonicalPackId(id);
92	    // A declaration mid-converge can carry BOTH spellings. Today's wins: it is the
93	    // one the flows have written, and the legacy key is the residue they replace.
94	    if (to !== id && Object.hasOwn(packVersions, to)) continue;
95	    out[to] = version;
96	  }
97	  return out;
98	}

1	// The `barriers` pack was absorbed into `basics` (#1681). Its check, its
2	// contribution seam and its guide moved; the engine's rename map resolves the id,
3	// so a member's packs activate correctly whether or not this record has run.
4	//
5	// WHAT ONLY THIS RECORD CAN DO is the declaration's SHAPE. The rename map moves an
6	// id; it does not move the parameters underneath one, and a repo's folder-access
7	// graph is exactly that — an array the owner wrote, which no reader could relocate
8	// on its own without inventing a second place to look for it forever. So the
9	// entry's `config` nests under `barriers` on the surviving `basics` entry, which
10	// is where the absorbed check now reads it.
11	//
12	// The recorded `goals` answer goes with it. It answered the barriers pack's one
13	// adoption question, which #1681 removed — the pack was never chosen (no
14	// fingerprint, pulled in by `requires` everywhere the baseline is declared), so the
15	// interview was guiding an adoption that never happened. Left in place it would
16	// read as an answer to a question `basics` does not ask, which is an
17	// interview-hygiene finding with no edit that clears it.
18	//
19	// GATED ON THE MOUNT, BY CONTENT. The nesting is `absorbedPackConfig`, a named op in
20	// the ENGINE's registry, and an engine that predates it would run the rename and skip
21	// the nesting — leaving the graph flat on the basics entry where nothing reads it, a
22	// silently unenforced barrier. So `appliesTo` probes the member's own mounted registry
23	// for the op rather than trusting a version; an unreadable mount reads as "not
24	// capable". The canon runs the same probe against its own tree (two-root form).
25	//
26	// WHAT SATISFIES THAT GATE IS RUN ORDER, NOT A RELEASE. A member's converge clones
27	// canon HEAD and replaces its engine subtree wholesale, whatever `ENGINE_VERSION`
28	// says, and the engine flow runs BEFORE the pack flow (tasks/update/worker.mjs) so
29	// that packs are never checked against yesterday's engine. So the op is already in the
30	// mount by the time this record runs, on the same converge that delivers it.
31	//
32	// WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE THERE IS ONLY ONE SHOT. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`
33	// against the stamped pack version, and pack-update stamps this pack at the manifest's
34	// number in the same run that applies its records. A cycle where the gate read false
35	// would stamp anyway, and the record would be out of range — and out of the vendor set
36	// — from then on, with nothing to bring it back but a redelivery record (#1545 is that
37	// repair done once already). The ordering above is what keeps that from happening.
38	//
39	// NOTHING DEPENDS ON THIS HAVING RUN. The rename map resolves the id and the
40	// absorbed check keeps a legacy read of the old placement until #1682, so a member
41	// is correct either way. What it buys is the day both tolerances can come out.
42	const REGISTRY = 'engine/migrations/registry.mjs';
43	const mountNestsAbsorbedConfig = async (read) => {
44	  const text = (await read(`.claudinite/shared/${REGISTRY}`)) ?? (await read(REGISTRY));
45	  return Boolean(text) && text.includes('absorbedPackConfig');
46	};
47	
48	export default {
49	  id: 'barriers-absorbed',
50	  landed: '2026-09-04',
51	  version: '60904.1',
52	  summary: 'the barriers pack is absorbed into basics (#1681) — the declared entry is renamed and its folder-access graph nests under `config.barriers` on the basics entry',
53	
54	  appliesTo: mountNestsAbsorbedConfig,
55	
56	  // The ids come from the engine's rename map (renamed-packs.mjs); this record adds
57	  // only what the map cannot say — that `barriers` was absorbed rather than
58	  // renamed, so its parameters nest and its answer is retired with its question.
59	  renameDeclaredPacks: true,
60	  absorbedPackConfig: [{ id: 'barriers', dropAnswers: ['goals'] }],
61	};

2	// were retired with the two per-object skills they applied; its comment pass, that
3	// pass's skill and the `improve-comments-scope` gate moved into the baseline.
4	//
5	// WHAT ONLY THIS RECORD CAN DO is converge the declaration. The rename map resolves
6	// the id at read time, so a member reads correctly whether or not this has run; what
7	// the record buys is the day the map can come out — and, before that, a declaration
8	// that says what is actually on the shelf rather than a pack directory nothing holds.
9	//
10	// NO `absorbedPackConfig`. That op nests an absorbed entry's parameters under the
11	// survivor's `config`, which is what a pack with parameters needs. `tidy-repo` asked
12	// no adoption question and read no config, so its entry is a bare id everywhere and
13	// the rename plus the duplicate-merge in `applyPackRenames` is the whole change.

20	// reason that absorption's record does: what it rewrites is the member's declaration,
21	// which is this pack's surface. A record's version must also sit at or below its own
22	// pack's, and a pending record above `basics`'s number would ride into a FRESH

24	// fetches whatever still applies above it, and an install must carry no records at

34	  // a record that falls at or below the installed version is silently already done.

    Retire the 2026-08-19 pack id tolerances from the rename map (#1916)
    
    * Retire the 2026-08-19 pack id tolerances from the rename map
    
    The seven spellings the 2026-08-19 renames and collapses left — core,
    grow_with_claudinite, chrome-extension-release, github-actions,
    firebase-release, canary-probe and sheepdog — come out of RENAMED_PACKS.
    Their convergence window closed a week after legacy-shape-in-use started
    reporting them, which is the gate: not a census of who still declares one,
    which the canon cannot read.
    
    The two absorptions that landed after that advisory shipped stay, each
    waiting out its own week (#1909): barriers -> basics and tidy-repo -> basics.
    Because both are absorptions, applyPackRenames and the canonicalization
    helpers stay with them — merging an absorbed entry into its survivor's is
    exactly what that op is for — so the map's retirement gate is now stated per
    entry rather than as one shared window.
    
    Every reader that resolved only a retired spelling goes: the sheepdog records'
    appliesTo gates and the fleet config's entry lookup, which now match today's id
    alone. The rename records' claim that nothing depends on them having run was
    true only while the tolerance stood, so each says so in the past tense and
    names what a member that never ran it now gets: no pack at all.
    
    Refs #1641
    Refs #1909
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FGq5yPVdbsxEP2H9v9WBQY
    
    * Keep the rename-map barrier for the one rename that outlived this branch
    
    This branch retired the 2026-08-19 tolerances and dropped the whole
    renamed-packs.mjs entry from the barrier exceptions with them. Since it was
    written, #2101 added `'static-website': 'public-website'` to the same map,
    so the file still names a barred pack folder and the exception is still
    earned - narrowed to the one pack that survives rather than the seven the
    entry used to carry.

input.title: Retire the `static-website` pack id tolerance, and the rename map with it
input.body:
Blocked-by: #1909
Not-before: 2026-09-28T09:00:00Z
Model: opus
Automerge: nothing

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

The tail of #1909, which took `barriers` and `tidy-repo` out of `RENAMED_PACKS`
(`engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs`) and left the one entry that landed *after* #1909 was
written: `static-website` → `public-website` (#2101, record dated 2026-09-17, added to the map
2026-09-21). #1909 could not take it out — its own convergence window was one day old on the day
that run went.

**The gate is the window, not a census.** `legacy-shape-in-use` started reporting the spelling on
2026-09-21, so the window closes 2026-09-28. Do not look for a count of who still declares it —
the canon cannot see which repos are active, inert or abandoned, and a removal waiting on that
answer never happens.

**The rest of #1641's ask belongs here**, because it only becomes available once the map is
empty: drop `applyPackRenames` (`engine/migrations/registry.mjs`) together with the
`renameDeclaredPacks` record field it reads, and the canonicalization callers that exist only for
it — `canonicalPackId`, `canonicalPackIdAmong`, `canonicalPackVersions` and their call sites.
#1909 could not do that half either: a live rename entry is exactly what `applyPackRenames`
converges. (`reshapeAbsorbed` and the `absorbedPackConfig` record field went out with the two
absorptions in #1909 — nothing left in the map was one.)

**Why `Automerge: nothing`**, unchanged from #1641 and #1909: a repo holding a retired spelling
beside a renamed mount activates *no* pack, so it loses its `update` task and the only route back
is a hand-run against that repo. Never widen this policy to fit the diff.

**Done looks like**: `RENAMED_PACKS` is empty or gone, the canonicalization surface goes with it,
and `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` is green. If a further rename has entered the map
by the time this runs, take out only the entries whose own week has passed and re-file this tail
behind the newest one — the window is per entry.

Part of #1638.

_Filed by the Claudinite task `claudinite-tasks/implement-request`, running as work item missingbulb/Claudinite#1909 — no person asked for this issue._

[claudinite sub-issue-without-parent] an issue filed under another ("Blocked-by: #1909") with no parent_issue_number. a child issue linked only by a number in its body leaves the parent blind to what is still open under it. Fix: pass parent_issue_number on the create, or attach it afterwards with sub_issue_write (method add, sub_issue_id the id the create returned, not its number)

{"number":1638,"title":"Retire Claudinite's live legacy tolerances","body":"Tracker for removing every legacy tolerance the engine and packs still carry. The mechanism that
makes each one visible and annotated is #1637; this is the removal half.

## What is still tolerated

| Family | Sites | What holds the old shape |
|---|---|---|
| Member declaration & stamp | `engine/settings-file-names.mjs`, `engine/installed-versions.mjs`, `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`, `engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs`, `engine/version.mjs` | a repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` name, `claudinite`/`maintenance` blocks, top-level `packConfig`, `taskScheduler.endpoints`, `local_packs/` declaration prefix, integer versions in a stamp |
| Renamed / absorbed pack ids | `engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs` | a repo declaring `core`, `grow_with_claudinite`, `sheepdog`, `canary-probe`, `chrome-extension-release`, `github-actions`, `firebase-release` |
| Task contract & queue vocabulary | `packs/claudinite-tasks/task-contract.mjs`, `run-record.mjs`, `queue/work-item.mjs`, `queue/secrets-bag.mjs`, `tasks/usage-fold/` | a repo's local-pack task declaring `agent_preprocessing`/`prework`/`after`/`self`; open work items wearing `task:*` labels; folded counters under old keys |
| Assorted residues | `packs/chrome-extension/worldRules/release-workflows.mjs`, `engine/served-by.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/engine-update.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-tasks/calendar.mjs`, `engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs` | a repo's release workflow, `servedBy: updates`, a stale vendored worker, a repo's `declared-checks.json` spellings |

## The gate is a window, not a census

*(Owner decision, 2026-09-03 — this replaces the plan's original first link, #1639, which is
closed.)*

Every one of these was originally gated on "no member still carries the shape", and the canon
cannot answer that: it does not know which repos that use it are active, which are inert, and
which stopped converging months ago. A gate phrased that way can never read true, which is how a
tolerance becomes permanent while looking scheduled.

So each removal is gated on a **convergence window** instead. The advisory ships with #1637; a
repo behaving correctly converges, sees its own finding and cleans up after itself within a week;
a week later the link releases and the tolerance comes out. A repo that has not converged in a
week is not being served by this canon whatever a census would have said. Later this may ride
major version releases instead.

Two decoders are the exception, and only because their gate is readable *here*: the `task:*`
labels drain as open work items close, and the folded counters drain with the retention window.
#1642 reads those two locally.

Getting a window wrong is not symmetric. For the first two families a repo that missed it gets
**no pack** rather than a degraded one, loses the `update` task that would have delivered its own
repair, and the only route back is a hand-run against that repo (`renamed-packs.mjs` states this).
Those two are `Automerge: nothing` whatever their diff looks like. #1642 carries a narrow
predicted-folder policy; #1643 stays `nothing` because it spans four packs by construction.

## The chain

- [ ] #1637 — the guideline, the site annotation and the advisories that tell a holder to move
- [x] ~~#1639 — fleet clearance report~~ — closed, not planned: see above
- [ ] #1640 — member declaration & stamp shapes
- [ ] #1641 — renamed / absorbed pack ids
- [ ] #1642 — task contract & queue vocabulary
- [ ] #1643 — assorted residues

Each removal is an ad-hoc queue item behind #1637 with `Not-before: 2026-09-10`. Nothing here is
on anyone's memory, and nothing waits on an answer the canon cannot get.

entries.description: Add a sub-issue to a parent issue in a GitHub repository.

after_id.description: The ID of the sub-issue to be prioritized after (either after_id OR before_id should be specified)

before_id.description: The ID of the sub-issue to be prioritized before (either after_id OR before_id should be specified)

issue_number.description: The number of the parent issue

method.description:
The action to perform on a single sub-issue
Options are:
- 'add' - add a sub-issue to a parent issue in a GitHub repository.
- 'remove' - remove a sub-issue from a parent issue in a GitHub repository.
- 'reprioritize' - change the order of sub-issues within a parent issue in a GitHub repository. Use either 'after_id' or 'before_id' to specify the new position.
Writes issue hierarchy. To move a sub-issue to a new parent, use `add` with `replace_parent=true`; there is no writable parent field.

replace_parent.description: When true, replaces the sub-issue's current parent issue. Use with 'add' method only.

sub_issue_id.description: The ID of the sub-issue to add. ID is not the same as issue number

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
  (see-test-fail)
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
  (mechanism-meant-survive)
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
  (simulator-stateful-mechanism)
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
  (trusting-new-transform)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
  (test-stubs-exact)
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
  (test-dereferences-path)
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
  (test-value-set)
- **Naming the thing a fixture stands for** - invent the name (`acme-pack`, `acme-user`,
  `acme.example`) wherever the case holds for any name at all, and keep a real one only where that
  entity is what the case asserts about: a borrowed name reads as meaningful, collides with the
  real thing's own cases, and makes every later rename an edit of tests that were never about it.
  (fixture-names-invented)
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite. (testing-tasks-precondition)
- **Asserting on a record the code under test produced** — a finding, a parsed spec, a normalized declaration — assert the fields that code **computed**, and leave the ones it copied straight through from its own declaration or from your setup. A check selected by its id whose test then reads `finding.rule` back, or restates the `severity` its declaration set, is asserting the selector: it stays green however wrong the matching is, and goes red only when someone deliberately renames or re-grades the rule. One computed field identifies a record — the rest is your setup talking back to you.
  (asserting-record-code)
- **A coupling that must hold for every member of a set** — each task's id matching the directory it is discovered by, each check's `doc:` pointer resolving, each declaration validating — assert it once in a sweep that reads the whole set out of the tree, never in each member's own suite. The per-member copy only ever holds the members that happen to have a suite, so it under-covers and taxes at the same time: the shape is billed to each suite that has one while the members without one go unguarded.
  (coupling-must-hold)
- **Pinning the text a finding or error carries** — assert the part the code **derived** from the input (the version it tells you to bump to, the path it resolved, the term it names), and leave the static sentence alone. A remedy's wording is prose someone will improve, and asserted back it turns every rewording into a test edit while guarding nothing — those words were read straight out of the declaration the test already points at.
  (pinning-text-finding)
- **Sweeping a set** — a tree walk, a filter over a file's lines, a loop over discovered
  members — **pin how many members it covered**, beside the loop. An assertion reached only
  inside a loop, or only behind an `if`, says nothing about the members that never entered it,
  so a set that quietly shrinks — a renamed token, a moved directory, one call kind of two
  dropping out — leaves the survivors passing and reports that pass for the whole. A count read
  off the same source is the pin (`assert.ok(files.length >= 25)`), and a guard *inside* the
  loop needs its own, since the
  outer count says nothing about how many members reached the assertion behind it. (sweeping-set)
- **Reading the source *text* of a module the test could `import`** — asserting an identifier
  appears in it, or that one string precedes another in the file — inverts the signal: it goes
  red on a pure rename and stays green on a behaviour change that leaves the tokens in place.
  Grepping a *different* artifact is the two-artifact drift guard above and stays. Where the
  module is callable and a grep is still the only way in, report that its entry point does the
  whole job at once — that is worth more than the assertion. (reading-source-text)
- **Choosing the cases for a validator, parser or guard** — its own rejection branches are the
  list: for each, write the input that forces it. A branch nothing forces is either a promise
  no test holds or one the code can no longer reach, and both are worth finding. The gap
  clusters on the **present-but-unusable** input — the empty string, the directory that will
  not read, the module that throws on import — because absent and valid are the two cases
  everyone writes, while the field that is there and broken is the one that arrives in
  production. (choosing-cases-validator)
- **A comparison against a threshold, a deadline or an anchor instant** — test the value
  exactly **on** it, not only either side. `<=` and `<` differ on exactly one input, so a suite
  that samples comfortably around the boundary agrees with both and pins neither. Where a cron
  or a poll drives the comparison, that one input is the ordinary case rather than the edge: the
  run fires *at* the anchor. (comparison-against-threshold)
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
  (prefer-single-shared)
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
  (wire-format-encoding)
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism.
  (traceability-coverage-gate)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
  (golden-snapshot-test)
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
  (snapshot-golden-test-2)
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
  (round-trip-test)
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
  (new-e2e-heavy)
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
  (test-can-only)
- **A shared fixture helper is paid for by every test that calls it**, so build the part that is identical for every case — a scratch repo's `init` and seed commit, a migrated database, a compiled bundle — once per process and copy it, rather than rebuilding it per test.
  (shared-fixture-helper)

- **A test runner parallelises across FILES, so one file's serial runtime is a floor no worker count clears.** When a suite's CPU sits well below its core count, the idle cores are waiting on that file — give it intra-file concurrency, which more workers cannot substitute for.
  (test-runner-parallelises)

- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
  (run-suite-know)
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically.
  (test-code-drives)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
  (gate-fuzzy-quality)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
  (behavior-person-must)
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
  (snapshot-golden-test)
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
  (test-asserts-exact)
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
  (test-maintains-committed)
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
  (render-ui-image)
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
  (reproduce-reported-golden)
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).
  (image-golden-surface)

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/running-the-suite

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — `packs/*/test/*.test.mjs` reports nothing wrong over 125 of 314 files — while
  `node --test <dir>` fails outright and a glob matching nothing exits 1, so only a glob that
  matches a subset leaves you believing a green run. (whole-suite-command)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (read-runs-output)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which.
  (git-add-new)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (iterating-sweep-across)
- **Editing a `RULES.md` or `README.md` under `packs/`** — the file that holds a pack's rule index
  in step with its prose sits outside the pack, and neither conformance sweep runs it, so add
  `node --test engine-tests/rule-index.test.mjs` to the files the edit touches. (editing-rules-md)
